poster.title: The Catcher in the Rye
poster.bookOrigin: American English-language novel by J.D. Salinger, first published in Boston in 1951.
poster.creator: E. Michael Mitchell
poster.alt: A red carousel horse with a bowed head at the right, flowing black tail at the upper left, and a thin pole dominates a tiny black city drawing; yellow title words fill the red upper field and black author lettering anchors the cream lower edge.
poster.blurb: An immense carousel horse turns a small city into a fragile background.

notes.title: The displayed edition

notes.title: Writing and image-making
notes.body: The Morgan Library & Museum credits the jacket design to E. Michael Mitchell. J.D. Salinger is the novelist; the Wikimedia file supplies the installed reproduction.

notes.title: A visible design relationship
notes.body: The horse’s flowing curves compete with straight title letters. Fine city marks require a closer look beneath the much broader red silhouette.

studyData.intro: A red carousel horse towers over a finely drawn city. This front panel keeps the horse and its visible pole together, allowing scale, line and publishing credits to be examined without inventing hidden drawing.

regions.label: A carousel horse fills the sheet
regions.summary: The broad red body extends across most of the front panel.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: The broad red body extends across most of the front panel. Dark curved outlines describe the belly, legs and decorative interior shapes.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The horse overwhelms the smaller city drawing and becomes the first pictorial encounter. Its scale is a design relationship, not a realistic comparison of objects.

regions.question: What kind of attention does the huge horse demand before you see the city?

regions.label: An arched neck ends in a bowed head
regions.summary: At the right, the horse bends its neck down into a bowed head.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: At the right, the horse bends its neck down into a bowed head. A small eye, bridle marks and muzzle distinguish the head from the legs beside it.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The downward turn gives the large animal a second direction within its broad horizontal body. Following the curved neck makes the head discoverable among the overlapping red forms.

regions.question: Which details distinguish the bowed head from the adjacent hanging leg?

regions.label: Fine movement over a red field
regions.summary: Long dark tail strokes run across the red upper field and approach the lower line of yellow title.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Long dark tail strokes run across the red upper field and approach the lower line of yellow title. Their curves overlap and change direction.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The tail makes a fluid counter-rhythm to the straighter letters. The shared space can make looking and reading compete without making either disappear.

regions.question: Which direction do the tail strokes lead you before the title interrupts?

regions.label: A bent leg ends in a hanging hoof
regions.summary: At the right, a red leg bends and narrows towards a dark-edged hoof.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: At the right, a red leg bends and narrows towards a dark-edged hoof. Cream gaps separate this limb from the belly and surrounding construction.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The suspended hoof helps distinguish a posed carousel animal from an animal standing firmly on ground. The reading comes from the visible support and pose together.

regions.question: What clues suggest that this horse belongs to a constructed ride?

regions.label: A small city under a large animal
regions.summary: Fine black building and landscape marks occupy the cream area below the horse.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Fine black building and landscape marks occupy the cream area below the horse. Their narrow strokes contrast with the broad red body above.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The change of scale rewards a second, slower look. The city can feel delicate because the large curves around it dominate so much of the available area.

regions.question: Would the city remain legible if its marks were as heavy as the horse’s outline?

regions.label: Yellow words across the red
regions.summary: The title is divided into large yellow lines across the red field.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: The title is divided into large yellow lines across the red field. Taller capitals share space with smaller words and the nearby tail strokes.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: Yellow against red gives the wording a clear colour identity. Varying letter sizes creates emphasis without adding a separate title box.

sections.heading: A title split for emphasis
sections.body: The English wording is kept intact even though its words are set at different sizes. Line division changes the reading rhythm without changing the title itself.

regions.question: Which word first catches your eye, and what makes it stronger than the others?

regions.label: The support passes through the picture
regions.summary: A narrow slanting pole runs behind and through the horse construction, with source-visible cream intervals and dark edges.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A narrow slanting pole runs behind and through the horse construction, with source-visible cream intervals and dark edges. Lower segments approach the author line.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The support makes the animal’s artificial setting more apparent. Keeping its visible run with the horse lets the construction remain intelligible when the layers open.

regions.question: What would you infer differently about the animal if this pole were absent?

regions.label: A novel and its author at the foot
regions.summary: Black wording identifies the book as a novel by J.D.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Black wording identifies the book as a novel by J.D. Salinger along the cream lower edge. The line is smaller than the title but has an uncluttered background.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The calmer strip provides a stopping point after the horse’s curves. It also changes from pictorial movement to the practical act of naming a writer.

sections.heading: Two different creative roles
sections.body: J.D. Salinger wrote the novel. The Morgan Library & Museum credits the jacket design to E. Michael Mitchell. Keeping these roles distinct avoids attributing the cover drawing to the novelist simply because his name is prominent on the front.

regions.question: How does the quiet background help this smaller line hold its own?

regions.label: Cream makes a second field
regions.summary: A pale cream field remains around the lower horse and author line.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A pale cream field remains around the lower horse and author line. It differs sharply from the saturated red upper field.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The broad colour division changes how the same red animal reads across the sheet. Its lower contours become more visible where red meets cream.

sections.heading: A specific jacket reproduction
sections.body: The installed image is the front panel of a first-edition jacket scan in Wikimedia Commons. Its contributor describes retouching, so this is a documented reproduction rather than an untouched archival capture. The full downloaded wrap is retained with the source record.

regions.question: Which part of the horse is easiest to follow against cream rather than red?

regions.label: Decorative loops inside the body
regions.summary: Curled dark lines form nested decorative shapes within the red body.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Curled dark lines form nested decorative shapes within the red body. These internal marks echo the tail while remaining enclosed by the animal’s silhouette.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The repeated curves make the horse feel ornamented as well as anatomical. They link the large silhouette to the finer surface activity near the title.

regions.question: How do the inner loops change the character of the broad red shape?

connections.label: Unequal scales
connections.title: A horse above a city
connections.text: The animal’s broad red curves dwarf the delicate city drawing.

connections.label: Movement and reading
connections.title: Tail against words
connections.text: Fine tail strokes flow close to the straight yellow letters, setting up competing rhythms.
